title: Civil rights
hookLine: Jews were among those who joined the American civil rights movement

cards: Three young civil rights workers drive out, one summer day in Mississippi, to look at a Black church that has been burned. They never come back. Days go by.
Their car is found in a swamp, burned too. James Chaney was a Black Mississippian. Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner were young Jewish men from New York.
All three were murdered by Klansmen. Their names are said together, and they belong together.

teach.b: The civil rights movement was led by Black Americans: preachers, students, sharecroppers, mothers, who faced its dangers every day.
Others came to stand with them, and Jews were among those who came. Some went south as volunteers to register voters. A group of rabbis was arrested in Florida for joining a protest.
Lawyers took cases; donors paid for bail. Why did they come? Some pointed to memory.
At every Passover, Jews tell the story of slavery in Egypt as their own, and the Torah says it plainly: "thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt."
Black churches had long sung the Exodus as their own story too, so the two communities shared a song.
Others pointed to the verse from Leviticus that came up with never again: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD." Here, not standing idly by meant going.
And the honest part: it was not a simple story. Some Southern Jews were afraid to speak up, and some agreed with segregation.
In later years, real tensions grew between some Black and Jewish leaders, alongside real friendships that lasted. So this isn't a trophy for anyone's shelf.
It's a record of people who chose not to stand idly by, and of the people who led them. Justice for all is a phrase Americans say about their own country. The movement asked the country to mean it.

how: Jewish communities remember the civil rights movement through the Torah's command not to stand idly by a neighbor's blood, and some synagogues hold joint services with Black churches around Martin Luther King Jr. Day.

games.q: you are a college student in New York. the movement asks for volunteers to register Black voters in Mississippi for the summer. it is dangerous. what do you do?
o: wait for the law to change on its own.
games.why: Andrew Goodman, one such student, went. soon after he arrived, he was murdered with James Chaney and Michael Schwerner.

practice: Go back to the car on that summer road, driving toward a church that had been burned, and think of what it takes to go toward a place like that, not away from it.
Then think of someone who stood up for another person's rights, well-known or not, a teacher, a grandparent, a neighbor, and hold their face for a while.
